segments.original: The 1990s and 2000s brought Latin American film classics and the rise of new directors who conquered box offices and awards around the world.
segments.text: The nineteen nineties and two thousands brought Latin American film classics and the rise of new directors who conquered box offices and awards around the world.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: With the arrival of the new millennium, Latin American cinema emerged as one of the best in the world. A generation of Mexican, Brazilian, Argentine, Chilean, and Peruvian filmmakers made films that captivated audiences in their own countries and around the globe. These directors won numerous awards, and some of them use their international standing to act as ambassadors for their respective national industries. In the early 1990s, such favorable circumstances would have been unimaginable.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In Mexico, years of poorly planned state intervention, along with distribution problems, had stripped the national cinema of its quality and its identity. By the mid-1990s, film production had fallen to the levels of the 1930s. Alfonso Cuarón (b. 1961) and Guillermo del Toro (b. 1964) were just two of the directors who stood out — with Solo con tu pareja (1992) and Cronos (1993) — but who felt that the only way forward was to leave for Hollywood.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The problems faced by the South American film industries were inextricably linked to the turbulent recent history of these societies. Dictatorships, institutionalized corruption, and ill-fated neoliberal experiments took their toll on cinema, including censorship, scarce funding, exile, and even murder. Add to this cultural turmoil on the continent the fact that thousands of movie theaters were converted into evangelical churches.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A bitter irony for Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico — the traditional powerhouses of Latin American cinema — was that their respective dictatorial governments were followed by democratically elected but philistine presidents who proved just as harmful to the national film industries as their predecessors. During President Fernando Collor de Mello's term, Brazil's film production shrank to a single feature film in three years, and in 1991 director Hector Babenco (b. 1946) declared, "Brazilian cinema is dead." That makes the country's subsequent comeback all the more extraordinary.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The countries of the continent share many political and social experiences, but their film output is understandably diverse. In Argentina, the region's largest source of world-class filmmakers, this variety is extraordinary. Pablo Trapero (b. 1971) epitomizes the talented generation that emerged from the country's newly founded state and private film schools. His realist style, which relies on non-professional actors and real-life subjects, has proved extremely versatile, ranging from his debut, Mundo grúa (1999), a bittersweet story of a middle-aged man trying to rebuild his life, through the road movie Familia rodante (Rolling Family, 2004), to the prison drama Leonera (Lion's Den, 2008).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Pan's Labyrinth may well be a grand summary of Mexican director Guillermo del Toro's career. He had worked on effects-heavy projects such as Hellboy (2004), and on others that build an atmosphere of suspense and tension while dealing with otherworldly matters, such as El espinazo del diablo (The Devil's Backbone, 2001). Pan's Labyrinth may be his most mature film. In it, the director manages to bring together his two particular strands. The result is a film that is at once dark and packed with effects.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Set against the backdrop of the period following the Spanish Civil War, the film's striking beauty and the strength of its performances offer the viewer many remarkable moments. "Pan's Labyrinth was a very difficult film," Del Toro told Sight & Sound magazine, "but it also became a battle over my commitment. I gave up my entire salary in order to make the film my way." If the story fails to fully merge reality and fantasy — Pan's Labyrinth consists of two separate halves rather than one spectacular whole — in the end, this does not make Del Toro's achievement any less extraordinary.

segments.original: The common denominator that unites all these directors is not their style but their attitude. With no interest in making genre films or aping Hollywood, they make personal films, true to their own experiences, concerns, and cinematic language. The school that has exerted the greatest influence on the continent is probably Neorealism. Although they are not polemical, these Latin American films shed light on the political, social, and even psychological problems of their countries, reflecting on what it means to be Latin American after years of struggle.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963) had such a strong and immediate effect on American filmmakers that it was only a matter of time before his influence spread to other countries. Amores Perros proves that by 2000 the Tarantino model of stylized violence and interwoven narratives had already made it south of the American border, to Mexico. The film marks the feature debut of Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu and, although the film ultimately offers nothing particularly new, his vibrant direction manages to inject energy, humor, intelligence, and tenderness into familiar plots.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Shot as three intertwined stories whose central characters meet at a certain key moment, Amores Perros stays true to the "canine" theme of its original title (Amores perros, in Spanish), as each segment of the film gives dogs a prominent role. In the first, a young man has an affair with his brother's wife and enters his prize dog in gruesome (and viscerally effective) fights in the hope of winning money to run away with his sister-in-law. In the second, a plot worthy of Edgar Allan Poe seen through the eyes of Luis Buñuel, a vain, crippled model loses her dog in a space beneath the floor of her apartment and is tormented by the sounds of the animal's incessant suffering, as well as by her inability to resolve the situation. In the last, a homeless hit man seeks redemption for the life he has led and recognition from his family, from whom he has long been estranged.

segments.original: All three segments ironically illustrate man's inhumanity to his fellow man through his treatment of animals, which in turn suffer so much in the film that Amores Perros displays a conspicuous notice that no animals were mistreated during the making of the film. In fact, the frequent violence of the dogs (and violence against the dogs) is portrayed so realistically that it sometimes threatens to overwhelm the film. But Iñárritu manages to convey his message of bloody betrayal, callous dishonesty, and class division with an abundance of style, revealing in the process a powerful confidence in his actors' instincts as well as in his audience's intelligence.

segments.original: In Venezuela, President Hugo Chávez seeks to take on "the dictatorship of Hollywood" with a new state-run studio, Villa del Cine, for the production of national feature films and documentaries. There are grants for independent filmmakers and exhibition laws to ensure that every Venezuelan film produced reaches the screen.

segments.original: A peaceful revolution is already sweeping Latin America — not political but cultural — one that promises to topple Hollywood's grip on movie theaters and popularize Latin American films with their domestic audiences. While this struggle continues, the best of these filmmakers are telling their stories in their own way and discovering that the rest of the world is watching.
